title: Deletes, versioning and re-embedding
summary: Deletes need a visible tombstone, versions need a rule for what the index keeps, and re-embedding needs a second index and an alias, because vectors from different models cannot be mixed.
useIf: Content is removed or superseded, a legal deletion deadline exists, or you will change embedding models during the life of the index.
avoidIf: The corpus is a frozen archive that is never edited or re-embedded: a simple one-time build is enough.

explain.md: **Deletes.** An indexer cannot see what the source silently removes. Blob has two soft-delete strategies: native blob soft delete (Blob Storage only, blob versioning must be off, retention well above the indexer interval) or a custom metadata flag such as `IsDeleted=true` followed by a physical delete. The policy must exist from the first run [[tr4]]. SQL uses `SoftDeleteColumnDeletionDetectionPolicy` [[tr5]] and Cosmos DB needs a top-level Boolean field [[tr6]]. Child chunks of a deleted parent are removed only when the data source has a deletion detection policy [[tr11]]. A reconciliation job is your proof that deletes happened.

**Versioning.** Decide whether the index holds only the latest version of a document or also history. Latest-only is simplest: replace on change. History needs fields such as `version` and `is_current` and a filter, and it raises ACL and storage questions.

**Re-embedding.** You cannot upgrade an embedding model in place, and vectors from different models are not comparable [[tr33]]. The query-time vectorizer must use the same model as the embedding skill [[tr12]]. So build a second index with the new model, keep both live while you validate, then repoint an **alias**, a service-level name that is separate from indexes [[tr10]]. Keep the old index through a rollback window. HNSW vectors consume memory quota, so two live copies roughly double that need [[tr41]].

explain.title: Blue-green re-embedding behind an alias
explain.alt: Applications query an alias that points at index v1. A backfill and dual-write fill index v2 with the new model, a quality gate checks it, and then the alias is repointed from v1 to v2.
explain.src:
flowchart LR
  A[App queries] --> L[Alias docs-live]
  L --> V1[(Index v1 old model)]
  B[Backfill and dual-write] --> V2[(Index v2 new model)]
  V2 --> Q[Quality gate]
  Q --> C[Repoint alias]
  C --> L

explain.title: Check retirement dates live
explain.md: The retirement schedule page (updated 2026-09-21) lists text-embedding-3-large, 3-small and ada-002 as retiring 2028-02-09. An older page said ada-002 retired no earlier than April 30, 2026. Check the live schedule before quoting a date [[tr32]].

whereToUse: Compliance-driven removal of documents within a stated deadline
Knowledge bases where policies are superseded and old versions must not be answered from
Changing the embedding model, dimensions or chunking strategy of a live index
Planning capacity for the period when two indexes are live
Release processes that need a tested rollback

use: Use soft-delete flags or native soft delete with a policy set before the first run
Use blue-green with an alias for any user-facing re-embedding
Use dual-write or a checkpointed replay so changes made during the backfill reach the new index
Keep the old index through a rollback window and quality checks
avoid: Avoid relying on physical deletes in the source for indexers that cannot detect them
Avoid re-embedding in place: there is no mixed-model state that works
Avoid deleting the old index before the new one has passed evaluation
flips: Downtime is acceptable and the corpus is small: rebuild in place during a maintenance window
Memory headroom is tight: stage the cutover by partition or add capacity for the overlap, because two live HNSW copies roughly double the memory need
Retirement date approaches: schedule the migration with margin, not at the deadline

pitfalls.symptom: Search returns nonsense after the model change
pitfalls.cause: The query vectorizer still uses the old model while the index holds new-model vectors
pitfalls.fix: Change the vectorizer with the index and test with known queries before the alias moves

pitfalls.symptom: Deleted parent documents leave orphan chunks
pitfalls.cause: Projected child chunks are removed only if the data source has a deletion detection policy
pitfalls.fix: Add the policy and verify with a reconciliation count

pitfalls.symptom: No way back after a bad cutover
pitfalls.cause: The old index was dropped right after the alias moved
pitfalls.fix: Keep it through a rollback window, then delete

pitfalls.symptom: The build of the new index fails on capacity
pitfalls.cause: HNSW vectors use memory quota and two copies double the need
pitfalls.fix: Check vector index size before starting and plan capacity for both

scenarios.title: Model migration for a customer-facing index
scenarios.situation: A production assistant uses an index of 20 million chunks. A new embedding model improves retrieval on the evaluation set. The assistant cannot go down and a quick rollback must exist.
constraints: Memory headroom exists for two copies
unknowns: How many changes arrive during the backfill?
How long is the overlap affordable?
scenarios.question: How do you migrate?

options.name: New index with the new model behind an alias, dual-write during backfill, quality gate, then repoint
options.why: Users keep the old index until the new one passes evaluation, and rollback is a repoint.
options.tradeoff: Double vector storage and a dual-write path for a while.

options.name: Add a second vector field to the same index and switch queries by flag
options.why: Keeps one index and one set of filters, with gradual cutover.
options.tradeoff: One index carries both vector sets, so memory and cleanup are harder to reason about.

options.name: Rebuild in place during a weekend window
options.why: It takes the service down and leaves no safe fallback if quality regresses.
options.tradeoff: Right for a small internal tool that tolerates downtime.

flips.then: Stage the migration by partition or add capacity for the overlap.

flips.if: The corpus is a few thousand chunks

scenarios.takeaway: Treat a model change like a database migration with a cutover and a way back.

scenarios.title: A 24 hour removal deadline from Blob Storage
scenarios.situation: Documents stored in Blob Storage must disappear from search within 24 hours of a removal request. The indexer runs every hour. Blob versioning is enabled for other reasons.
unknowns: Who sets the flag and how is it audited?
Are there copies in caches or exports?
scenarios.question: How do you implement deletes?

options.name: Custom metadata flag such as `IsDeleted=true`, indexer deletion policy, physical delete after the run, plus reconciliation
options.why: It works with versioning on, is visible to the indexer and leaves an audit trail.
options.tradeoff: The convention must be enforced and the physical delete must wait for the indexer.

options.name: Native blob soft delete
options.why: Native soft delete needs blob versioning off, which is not the case here.
options.tradeoff: Right when versioning is off and retention exceeds the indexer interval.

options.name: Delete blobs directly and wait
options.why: The indexer cannot see hard deletes by default, so entries stay in the index.
options.tradeoff: Right only with a reconciliation job that removes the orphans.

flips.then: Native soft delete with long retention is simpler.
Delete from the index directly through the push API as part of the removal workflow.

scenarios.takeaway: Pick the delete signal that your source and settings allow, and prove it with reconciliation.

quiz.q: What does an index alias let you do during re-embedding?
options: Mix old and new vectors in one field
Upgrade the embedding model in place
Repoint applications to a rebuilt index without code changes
quiz.explain: An alias is a service-level name you repoint to cut over. Mixing models in one field is invalid, in-place upgrades are not supported, and quality checks remain necessary.

quiz.q: Your live index uses 40 GB of vector index quota. You build an equal-size index with a new model and keep both live. What is the minimum vector quota you need, in GB?
quiz.explain: Two equal indexes need about 80 GB because HNSW graphs are held in memory. Real needs vary with the new model's dimensions and compression.

quiz.q: Which are true for blob delete handling in Azure AI Search?
options: Deletes are not tracked by default
Native soft delete requires blob versioning to be off
The policy can be added any time and corrects history
A custom metadata flag followed by a physical delete is supported
quiz.explain: Defaults ignore deletes, native soft delete needs versioning off, and a metadata flag is a supported strategy. The policy must exist from the first run, so it cannot correct history.

flashcards.front: Why can't you upgrade an embedding model in place?
flashcards.back: Vectors from different models are not comparable. Azure says you need new embeddings, so build a new index and switch an alias.

flashcards.front: Two soft-delete strategies for the Blob indexer?
flashcards.back: Native blob soft delete (versioning off, long retention) or a metadata flag like `IsDeleted=true` then physical delete. Policy must exist from the first run.

flashcards.front: What must match between the embedding skill and the index at query time?
flashcards.back: The vectorizer's model must be the same as the embedding skill's model that produced the stored vectors.
